item.title: Cryptography Foundations
item.description: Cryptography applies mathematical primitives to security goals such as confidentiality, integrity, peer authentication, and non-repudiation. A secure primitive does not make a protocol secure by itself because encodings, key management, randomness, state, and the attacker’s capabilities also determine the result.

item.title: Cryptography Standards and Encodings
item.description:
Cryptographic names often identify an issuing organization and a document series. A protocol must name the exact version, algorithm identifiers, parameters, and encoding rules it implements; a broad label such as “PKCS” or “X.509” is insufficient.

ITU-T X-Series and X.509 #

The ITU Telecommunication Standardization Sector (ITU-T) publishes Recommendations in lettered series. The X-series covers data networks, open systems communications, and security. ITU-T X.509 defines a public-key certificate framework and an ASN.1 certificate structure. The IETF profiles X.509 certificates for Internet use in RFC 5280.

item.title: RSA Encryption and Signatures
item.description: RSA defines trapdoor operations on integers modulo a composite number. Secure systems use those operations only through standardized encryption or signature schemes because textbook RSA is deterministic, malleable, and structurally unsafe.

item.title: X.509 Certificates
item.description:
An X.509 certificate binds a subject public key to an asserted subject identity through an issuer signature. Certificate validation determines whether that binding is acceptable for a specific protocol and connection. Parsing a certificate or verifying its signature alone is not sufficient.

Encoding and Certificate Structure #

Certificates are ASN.1 values conventionally encoded with DER. PEM is the base64 text form of a DER object:

text 
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

The signed tbsCertificate contains a version, issuer-unique serial number, issuer distinguished name, validity interval, subject distinguished name, SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI), and extensions. The outer certificate also contains the issuer’s signature algorithm identifier and signature over tbsCertificate. The issuer public key is not embedded as a separate certificate field; it is found by constructing a path to an issuer certificate or trust anchor.

item.title: Cryptographic Hash Functions
item.description: Cryptographic hash functions reduce arbitrary byte strings to fixed-size digests. Protocols rely on specific resistance properties rather than on the mere act of hashing, because a fast unkeyed digest provides neither message authentication nor safe password storage.

item.title: Cryptographic Trust Stores
item.description: A trust store contains local trust anchors and, on some platforms, intermediate certificates or private-key entries. A verifier uses those anchors when it builds and validates an X.509 certification path. Installing a root therefore changes the security boundary of every client that reads that store.

item.title: OpenSSL Command-Line Guide
item.description:
OpenSSL provides cryptographic primitives, protocol libraries, and command-line tools. Commands are useful for inspection, interoperability tests, and local administration; application code should use a maintained language library and its safe defaults.

Keys, CSRs, and Certificates #

sh 
openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA \
 -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 \
 -out private-key.pem
openssl pkey -in private-key.pem -pubout -out public-key.pem

item.title: TLS 1.3
item.description:
This overview describes TLS 1.3. TLS carries a sequence of records. Before encryption, handshake data is carried in TLSPlaintext records; the legacy record-version field exists for interoperability and TLS 1.3 peers do not use it to negotiate the protocol. Records are limited to 2^14 bytes of content before permitted expansion.

Handshake #

The client sends ClientHello with a random value, supported cipher suites, key shares, extensions, and a legacy session ID. Its legacy_version is 0x0303; the supported-versions extension negotiates TLS 1.3. Current standard AEAD suites include AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 with SHA-256 or SHA-384.

item.title: JSON Canonicalization
item.description:
JSON canonicalization turns semantically equivalent JSON data into one deterministic byte sequence. It is useful before hashing, signing, comparing, or using JSON as an identity key. Ordinary JSON serialization is not enough: object-member order, whitespace, escaping, and number formatting can differ without changing the data model.

JSON Canonicalization Scheme #

RFC 8785 defines the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). It uses the ECMAScript JSON serialization rules, serializes object properties in lexicographic order of UTF-16 code units, emits no insignificant whitespace, and requires valid I-JSON input.
